Income falls into three brackets: first $11,000 at 10%, next $44,000 ($55,000 − $11,000) at 18%, and remaining $16,250 ($71,250 − $55,000) at 31%.

Tax = $11,000 × 10% + ($55,000 − $11,000) × 18% + ($71,250 − $55,000) × 31%
= $1,100 + $7,920 + $5,037.50
= $14,057.50

Check: 11,000 × 0.10 = 1,100; 44,000 × 0.18 = 7,920; 16,250 × 0.31 = 5,037.50; sum = 14,057.50.

The prompt's wording — "10% on the first $11,000", "18% on income above $11,000 up to $55,000", and "31% on income above $55,000" — explicitly defines each rate as applying only to the portion of income within that specific range, not to total income. This is the defining feature of a marginal/progressive bracket system, as opposed to a flat-rate tax where a single rate would apply to the whole income. A flat 31% interpretation contradicts the explicit phrase "on income above $55,000," which restricts that rate to income exceeding $55,000, not all income. Therefore the marginal interpretation is the only one consistent with the stated wording, and the flat-rate alternative is not a valid competing reading.

FINAL: 14057.50
